Everybody at this table has an opinion about the election. I am curious about yours — but first, where do you actually get your news?
Four outlets, deliberately. Two I agree with, two I do not. Anything that appears in only one of them, I follow closely before I repeat it.
That is more discipline than most journalists have. Does it change your mind often?
Rarely. But last year I was swayed by a piece on migration that I had every intention of disagreeing with.
Those are the good ones. What did it get right?
It refused to make a sweeping statement. Every number came with the reason it might be wrong.
You would be surprised how hard that is to sell to an editor. Most of them want a headline, not a caveat.
I can imagine. Although in hindsight, the pieces I still remember from the nineties were all written like that.
I follow four outlets, and two of them disagree with me on purpose.

Good evening. Before the main bulletin, a word about a story we have been following closely all week. On Tuesday, a regional paper in the north broke a story about three contracts signed without a public tender. By Thursday every national outlet had picked it up, and by Friday the minister involved had resigned. Two things are worth saying. First, the paper that broke it has eleven journalists. Second, the documents had been publicly available since March, and nobody had read them. Whatever you conclude about the politics, that part is not in dispute. We will have the full report at ten.

People ask me how we decide what goes on the front page, and they expect a grand answer. There isn't one. Every morning about fifteen of us sit in a room for forty minutes and argue. Somebody has a story that matters and nobody will read. Somebody else has a story that everybody will read and that changes nothing. The job is choosing between them, four times a week, under time pressure, with incomplete information. We get it wrong regularly. What I would say in our defense is this. When we get it wrong, you can see it, because it is printed with our names on it. That is more than most industries can offer. Read us with a grain of salt, by all means. But read more than one of us.

Diane asks where he actually gets his news, before she hears any opinion. He answers that he follows four outlets, two of which he chose to disagree with him. She says that is more discipline than most journalists have, and asks whether it changes his mind. He admits he was swayed by a piece on migration he had intended to disagree with. She explains that most editors want a headline rather than a caveat.
